e-4910.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given in Canonical Form
e-4910.problem: Consider the straight line with the canonical equation $\dfrac{x}{5}=\dfrac{y+3}{3}=\dfrac{z-2}{1}.$ Find the vector equation of the line.
e-4910.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ and is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}=\langle v_x, v_y, v_z \rangle$ is given by

$$
\dfrac{x-x_0}{v_x}=\dfrac{y-y_0}{v_y}=\dfrac{z-z_0}{v_z} = t, \qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\dfrac{x}{5}=\dfrac{y-(-3)}{3}=\dfrac{z-2}{1},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(0,-3,2)$ and is parallel to $\mathbf{v}=\langle 5,3,1 \rangle.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

e-4911.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given in Parametric or Vector Form
e-4911.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1-2t \\ y=4t \\ z=-2+3t\end{aligned}
$$

for $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
e-4911.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1-2t \\ 4t \\ -2+3t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2t \\ 4t \\ 3t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

This implies that the given line passes through the point $P(1,0,-2)$ and is parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}=\langle -2, 4, 3 \rangle.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{-2}=\dfrac{y}{4}=\dfrac{z-(-2)}{3} = t, 	\qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{-2}=\dfrac{y}{4}=\dfrac{z+2}{3}.
$$

e-5021.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line When a Component of the Direction Vector is Zero
e-5021.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14042625/assets/fea24c391122278ffe20ec0f6a7d704b835aca18c3bdcd7395aeeea0f593a2bf.png)
e-5021.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{4}=\dfrac{y-2}{0}=\dfrac{z-3}{5} = t,	\qquad t \in (-\infty,\infty),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{4}=\dfrac{y-2}{0}=\dfrac{z-3}{5},
$$

which is problematic because $\dfrac{y-2}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $y$ component always maintains the constant value of $y=2\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14042625/assets/368f42200b9366547bdff9840a894b63d3df43722052ecb1a4e15e2306b4e56a.png)

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\dfrac{y-2}{0}$ part and instead write $y=2,$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{x-1}{4}=\dfrac{z-3}{5}, \; y=2
$$

Consider the straight line with the canonical equation x−32=y−11=z+43. Find the vector equation of the line.

a

None of the listed

[−3−14]+t[213],t∈(−∞,∞)

decision.explanation: Set each ratio equal to t. Then x=3+2t, y=1+t, and z=-4+3t, so the line passes through (3,1,-4) with direction vector (2,1,3). This gives option d.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Consider the straight line with the canonical equation $\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z+4}{3}.$ Find the vector equation of the line.
after.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-(-4)}{3},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(3,1,-4)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,1,3⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Consider the straight line with the canonical equation x−32=y−11=z+43. Find the vector equation of the line.

a
t[213],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
None of the listed
c
[−3−14]+t[213],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
[31−4]+t[213],t∈(−∞,∞)
e
[213]+t[31−4],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point P(x0,y0,z0) and is parallel to the vector v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩, is given by x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vz=t,t∈(−∞,∞).

Comparing the above to our given equation x−32=y−11=z−(−4)3,

we find that our line passes through the point P(3,1,−4) and is parallel to v=⟨2,1,3⟩. Therefore, its vector equation is

r=p+tvr=[31−4]+t[213],t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given in Canonical Form
content.problem: Consider the straight line with the canonical equation $\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z+4}{3}.$ Find the vector equation of the line.
content.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-(-4)}{3},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(3,1,-4)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,1,3⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Setting the common ratio equal to t gives x=2+3t, y=1-2t, and z=-3+7t. Thus the position vector is (2,1,-3)+t(3,-2,7), matching option c.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find the vector equation of the line $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z+3}{7}.$
after.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-(-3)}{7}
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(2,1,-3)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨3,-2,7⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point P(x0,y0,z0) and is parallel to the vector v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩, is given by x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vz=t,t∈(−∞,∞).

Comparing the above to our given equation x−23=y−1−2=z−(−3)7

we find that our line passes through the point P(2,1,−3) and is parallel to v=⟨3,−2,7⟩. Therefore, its vector equation is

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given in Canonical Form
content.problem: Find the vector equation of the line $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z+3}{7}.$
content.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-(-3)}{7}
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(2,1,-3)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨3,-2,7⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

a
r=[47−6]+t[3−1−7],t∈(−∞,∞)
b

decision.explanation: Setting each ratio equal to t gives x=4+3t, y=7-t, and z=-6-7t. Thus the line has point (4,7,-6) and direction (3,-1,-7), matching option a.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Consider the straight line with the canonical equation $\frac{x-4}{3}=\frac{y-7}{-1}=\frac{z+6}{-7}.$ Find the vector equation of the line.
after.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\frac{x-4}{3}=\frac{y-7}{-1}=\frac{z-(-6)}{-7},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(4,7,-6)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨3,-1,-7⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 7 \\ -6\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ -7\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point P(x0,y0,z0) and is parallel to the vector v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩, is given by x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vz=t,t∈(−∞,∞).

Comparing the above to our given equation x−43=y−7−1=z−(−6)−7, we find that our line passes through the point P(4,7,−6) and is parallel to v=⟨3,−1,−7⟩. Therefore, its vector equation is

r=p+tvr=[47−6]+t[3−1−7],t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given in Canonical Form
content.problem: Consider the straight line with the canonical equation $\frac{x-4}{3}=\frac{y-7}{-1}=\frac{z+6}{-7}.$ Find the vector equation of the line.
content.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\frac{x-4}{3}=\frac{y-7}{-1}=\frac{z-(-6)}{-7},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(4,7,-6)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨3,-1,-7⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 7 \\ -6\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ -7\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Find the parametric equations of the line $\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-1}{4}=\frac{z+1}{3}.$
after.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-1}{4}=\frac{z-(-1)}{3},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(2,1,-1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,4,3⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations are the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2+2t \\ y=1+4t \\ z=-1+3t\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given in Canonical Form
content.problem: Find the parametric equations of the line $\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-1}{4}=\frac{z+1}{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-1}{4}=\frac{z-(-1)}{3},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(2,1,-1)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,4,3⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations are the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2+2t \\ y=1+4t \\ z=-1+3t\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the straight line with the canonical equation x1=y+12=z3. Find the vector equation of the line.

a
r=[123]+t[0−10],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
None of the listed
c
r=[0−10]+t[123],t∈(−∞,∞)

decision.explanation: Setting each ratio equal to t gives x=t, y=-1+2t, and z=3t. Thus the line passes through (0,-1,0) with direction (1,2,3), matching option c.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Consider the straight line with the canonical equation $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z}{3}.$ Find the vector equation of the line.
after.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y-(-1)}{2}=\frac{z}{3},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(0,-1,0)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨1,2,3⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider the straight line with the canonical equation x1=y+12=z3. Find the vector equation of the line.

a
r=[123]+t[0−10],t∈(−∞,∞)
b
None of the listed
c
r=[0−10]+t[123],t∈(−∞,∞)
d
r=t[123],t∈(−∞,∞)
e
r=t[0−10],t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point P(x0,y0,z0) and is parallel to the vector v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩, is given by x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vz=t,t∈(−∞,∞).

Comparing the above to our given equation x1=y−(−1)2=z3,

we find that our line passes through the point P(0,−1,0) and is parallel to v=⟨1,2,3⟩. Therefore, its vector equation is

r=p+tvr=[0−10]+t[123],t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Vector Equation of a Line Given in Canonical Form
content.problem: Consider the straight line with the canonical equation $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z}{3}.$ Find the vector equation of the line.
content.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Comparing the above to our given equation

$$
\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y-(-1)}{2}=\frac{z}{3},
$$

we find that our line passes through the point $P(0,-1,0)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨1,2,3⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Consider the straight line with the parametric equations {x=2+4ty=5+5tz=−1+6t for t∈(−∞,∞). Find the Cartesian equation of this line.

a
x2=y5=z−1
b
x−24=y−55=z+16
c
x−42=y−55=z−6−1
d
x+24=y−55=z−16
e
x4=y5=z6
Submit

decision.explanation: Solving each parametric equation for t gives t=(x-2)/4=(y-5)/5=(z+1)/6, matching option b.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2+4t \\ y=5+5t \\ z=-1+6t\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2+4t \\ 5+5t \\ -1+6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 5t \\ 6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(2,5,-1)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,5,6⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-5}{5}=\frac{z-(-1)}{6}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-5}{5}=\frac{z+1}{6}.
$$

Question 6

Consider the straight line with the parametric equations {x=2+4ty=5+5tz=−1+6t for t∈(−∞,∞). Find the Cartesian equation of this line.

a
x2=y5=z−1
b
x−24=y−55=z+16
c
x−42=y−55=z−6−1
d
x+24=y−55=z−16
e
x4=y5=z6
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows: [xyz]=[2+4t5+5t−1+6t][xyz]=[25−1]+[4t5t6t][xyz]=[25−1]+t[456]r=[25−1]+t[456], where t∈(−∞,∞).

This implies that the straight line passes through the point P(2,5,−1) and is parallel to the vector v=⟨4,5,6⟩. So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

x−24=y−55=z−(−1)6=t,t∈(−∞,∞). Simplifying, we reach x−24=y−55=z+16.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given in Parametric or Vector Form
content.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2+4t \\ y=5+5t \\ z=-1+6t\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
content.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2+4t \\ 5+5t \\ -1+6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 5t \\ 6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ -1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(2,5,-1)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,5,6⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-5}{5}=\frac{z-(-1)}{6}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-5}{5}=\frac{z+1}{6}.
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Consider the straight line with the vector equation

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ 9\end{aligned}]
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
after.worked_solution:
We have the vector equation 

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ 9\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(3,4,-5)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,6,9⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-3}{4}=\frac{y-4}{6}=\frac{z-(-5)}{9}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-3}{4}=\frac{y-4}{6}=\frac{z+5}{9}.
$$

r=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ -5\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6 \\ 9\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(3,4,-5)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,6,9⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-3}{4}=\frac{y-4}{6}=\frac{z-(-5)}{9}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-3}{4}=\frac{y-4}{6}=\frac{z+5}{9}.
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2+4t \\ y=-3+5t \\ z=7-6t\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2+4t \\ -3+5t \\ 7-6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 5t \\ -6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ -6\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

This implies that the given line passes through the point $P(2,-3,7)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,5,-6⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-(-3)}{5}=\frac{z-7}{-6}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y+3}{5}=\frac{z-7}{-6}.
$$

b

EXPLANATION

[xyz]=[2+4t−3+5t7−6t][xyz]=[2−37]+[4t5t−6t][xyz]=[2−37]+t[45−6]r=[2−37]+t[45−6], where t∈(−∞,∞).

This implies that the given line passes through the point P(2,−3,7) and is parallel to the vector v=⟨4,5,−6⟩. So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given in Parametric or Vector Form
content.problem:
Consider the straight line with the parametric equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2+4t \\ y=-3+5t \\ z=7-6t\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
content.worked_solution:
First, let's find the corresponding vector equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2+4t \\ -3+5t \\ 7-6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 5t \\ -6t\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\ r & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 5 \\ -6\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

This implies that the given line passes through the point $P(2,-3,7)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨4,5,-6⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-(-3)}{5}=\frac{z-7}{-6}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y+3}{5}=\frac{z-7}{-6}.
$$

Question 9
?

Consider the straight line with the vector equation r=[−233]+t[2−53]

for t∈(−∞,∞). Find the Cartesian equation of this line.

a
x−22=y+3−5=z−33
b
x+22=y−3−5=z−33
c
x−22=y+5−3=z−33
d
x−2−2=y+53=z−33
e
x+2−2=y−35=z+33
Submit

decision.explanation: The vector equation gives x=-2+2t, y=3-5t, and z=3+3t. Solving for t yields (x+2)/2=(y-3)/(-5)=(z-3)/3, matching option b.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Consider the straight line with the vector equation

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
after.worked_solution:
We have the vector equation 

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(-2,3,3)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨2,-5,3⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-(-2)}{2}=\frac{y-3}{-5}=\frac{z-3}{3}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac{y-3}{-5}=\frac{z-3}{3}.
$$

after.html:
Question 9
?

Consider the straight line with the vector equation r=[−233]+t[2−53]

for t∈(−∞,∞). Find the Cartesian equation of this line.

a
x−22=y+3−5=z−33
b
x+22=y−3−5=z−33
c
x−22=y+5−3=z−33
d
x−2−2=y+53=z−33
e
x+2−2=y−35=z+33
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We have the vector equation r=[−233]+t[2−53],t∈(−∞,∞).

This implies that the straight line passes through the point P(−2,3,3) and is parallel to the vector v=⟨2,−5,3⟩. So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

x−(−2)2=y−3−5=z−33=t,t∈(−∞,∞).

Simplifying, we reach x+22=y−3−5=z−33.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given in Parametric or Vector Form
content.problem:
Consider the straight line with the vector equation

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
content.worked_solution:
We have the vector equation 

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(-2,3,3)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨2,-5,3⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-(-2)}{2}=\frac{y-3}{-5}=\frac{z-3}{3}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac{y-3}{-5}=\frac{z-3}{3}.
$$

Question 10
?

Consider the straight line with the vector equation r=[7−24]+t[1−23]

for t∈(−∞,∞). Find the Cartesian equation of this line.

a
x−17=y+2−2=z−34
b
x+17=y+2−2=z−3−4
c
x−71=y+2−2=z−43
d
x+71=y+2−2=z−34
e
x−73=y+2−2=z−41
Submit

decision.explanation: The vector equation gives x=7+t, y=-2-2t, and z=4+3t. Solving each for t yields (x-7)/1=(y+2)/(-2)=(z-4)/3, matching option c.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Consider the straight line with the vector equation

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
after.worked_solution:
We have the vector equation 

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(7,-2,4)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨1,-2,3⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-7}{1}=\frac{y-(-2)}{-2}=\frac{z-4}{3}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-7}{1}=\frac{y+2}{-2}=\frac{z-4}{3}.
$$

after.html:
Question 10
?

Consider the straight line with the vector equation r=[7−24]+t[1−23]

for t∈(−∞,∞). Find the Cartesian equation of this line.

a
x−17=y+2−2=z−34
b
x+17=y+2−2=z−3−4
c
x−71=y+2−2=z−43
d
x+71=y+2−2=z−34
e
x−73=y+2−2=z−41
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We have the vector equation r=[7−24]+t[1−23],t∈(−∞,∞).

This implies that the straight line passes through the point P(7,−2,4) and is parallel to the vector v=⟨1,−2,3⟩. So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

x−71=y−(−2)−2=z−43=t,t∈(−∞,∞).

Simplifying, we reach x−71=y+2−2=z−43.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given in Parametric or Vector Form
content.problem:
Consider the straight line with the vector equation

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

for $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ Find the Cartesian equation of this line.
content.worked_solution:
We have the vector equation 

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

This implies that the straight line passes through the point $P(7,-2,4)$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨1,-2,3⟩.$ So, its Cartesian (canonical) equation is given by

$$
\frac{x-7}{1}=\frac{y-(-2)}{-2}=\frac{z-4}{3}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Simplifying, we reach

$$
\frac{x-7}{1}=\frac{y+2}{-2}=\frac{z-4}{3}.
$$

Question 11
?

Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

r=[−350]+t[0−21],t∈(−∞,∞)

a
x+3=z,y=5
b
x−3=y+25,z=1
c
y+5−2=z,x=3
d
y−5−2=z,x=−3
e
x+3=y−5−2=z
Submit

decision.explanation: The vector equation gives x=-3, y=5-2t, and z=t. Eliminating t yields (y-5)/(-2)=z with x=-3, matching option d.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
after.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-(-3)}{0}=\frac{y-5}{-2}=\frac{z-0}{1}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+3}{0}=\frac{y-5}{-2}=z,
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{x+3}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $x$ component always maintains the constant value of $x=-3:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5-2t \\ t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{x+3}{0}$ part and instead write $x=-3,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{y-5}{-2}=z,\,x=-3
$$

\frac{x+3}{0}=\frac{y-5}{-2}=z,

which is problematic because $\frac{x+3}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $x$ component always maintains the constant value of $x=-3:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5-2t \\ t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{x+3}{0}$ part and instead write $x=-3,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{y-5}{-2}=z,\,x=-3
$$

Question 12
?

Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

r=[−321]+t[30−2],t∈(−∞,∞)

a
 x−33=z−1−2,y=−2
b
 x−33=z+1−2,y=2
c
 x+33=z−1−2,y=2
d
 x+33=z+1−2,y=−2
e
 x+3−3=z−12,y=2
Submit

decision.explanation: The vector equation gives x=-3+3t, y=2, and z=1-2t, so (x+3)/3=(z-1)/(-2), y=2. This is option c. Option e is also equivalent because both denominators are negated; c is the direct construction.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
after.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-(-3)}{3}=\frac{y-2}{0}=\frac{z-1}{-2}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+3}{3}=\frac{y-2}{0}=\frac{z-1}{-2},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{y-2}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $y$ component always maintains the constant value of $y=2:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-3+3t \\ 2 \\ 1-2t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{y-2}{0}$ part and instead write $y=2,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x+3}{3}=\frac{z-1}{-2},\,y=2
$$

after.html:
Question 12
?

Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

r=[−321]+t[30−2],t∈(−∞,∞)

a
 x−33=z−1−2,y=−2
b
 x−33=z+1−2,y=2
c
 x+33=z−1−2,y=2
d
 x+33=z+1−2,y=−2
e
 x+3−3=z−12,y=2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the usual formula, we get

x−(−3)3=y−20=z−1−2=t,t∈(−∞,∞),

or equivalently

x+33=y−20=z−1−2,

which is problematic because y−20 involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the y component always maintains the constant value of y=2:

r=[−3+3t21−2t],t∈(−∞,∞)

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the y−20 part and instead write y=2, as follows:

x+33=z−1−2,y=2

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line When a Component of the Direction Vector is Zero
content.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
content.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-(-3)}{3}=\frac{y-2}{0}=\frac{z-1}{-2}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+3}{3}=\frac{y-2}{0}=\frac{z-1}{-2},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{y-2}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $y$ component always maintains the constant value of $y=2:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-3+3t \\ 2 \\ 1-2t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{y-2}{0}$ part and instead write $y=2,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x+3}{3}=\frac{z-1}{-2},\,y=2
$$

Question 13
?

Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

r=[7−911]+t[−320],t∈(−∞,∞)

a
x−7−3=y+92=z−11
b
x−7−3=z−11,y=−9
c
x+7−3=y−92,z=−11
d
x−7−3=y+92,z=11
e
x+37=y−2−9,z=0
Submit

decision.explanation: The vector equation gives x=7-3t, y=-9+2t, and z=11. Eliminating t yields (x-7)/(-3)=(y+9)/2 with z=11, matching option d.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -9 \\ 11\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
after.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-7}{-3}=\frac{y-(-9)}{2}=\frac{z-11}{0}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-7}{-3}=\frac{y+9}{2}=\frac{z-11}{0},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{z-11}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $z$ component always maintains the constant value of $z=11:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}7-3t \\ -9+2t \\ 11\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{z-11}{0}$ part and instead write $z=11$, as follows:

$$
\frac{x-7}{-3}=\frac{y+9}{2},\,z=11
$$

Question 13
?

Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

r=[7−911]+t[−320],t∈(−∞,∞)

a
x−7−3=y+92=z−11
b
x−7−3=z−11,y=−9
c
x+7−3=y−92,z=−11
d
x−7−3=y+92,z=11
e
x+37=y−2−9,z=0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Using the usual formula, we get

x−7−3=y−(−9)2=z−110=t,t∈(−∞,∞),

or equivalently

x−7−3=y+92=z−110,

which is problematic because z−110 involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the z component always maintains the constant value of z=11:

r=[7−3t−9+2t11],t∈(−∞,∞)

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the z−110 part and instead write z=11, as follows:

x−7−3=y+92,z=11

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option d. Since x=7-3t, y=-9+2t, and z=11, eliminating t gives (x-7)/(-3)=(y+9)/2 with z=11. The observed incorrect submission selected e.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line When a Component of the Direction Vector is Zero
content.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -9 \\ 11\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
content.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-7}{-3}=\frac{y-(-9)}{2}=\frac{z-11}{0}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-7}{-3}=\frac{y+9}{2}=\frac{z-11}{0},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{z-11}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $z$ component always maintains the constant value of $z=11:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}7-3t \\ -9+2t \\ 11\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{z-11}{0}$ part and instead write $z=11$, as follows:

$$
\frac{x-7}{-3}=\frac{y+9}{2},\,z=11
$$

Question 14
?

Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

r=[3−16]+t[7−30],t∈(−∞,∞)

a
x−37=y+1−3,z=6
b
x−73=y+3−1,z=0
c
x+37=y−1−3,z=−6
d
x+73=y−3−1,z=0
e
x−37=y+1−3=z−6
Submit

decision.explanation: The vector equation gives x=3+7t, y=-1-3t, and z=6. Eliminating t yields (x-3)/7=(y+1)/(-3), with z=6, matching option a.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
after.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-3}{7}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-3}=\frac{z-6}{0}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-3}{7}=\frac{y+1}{-3}=\frac{z-6}{0},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{z-6}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $z$ component always maintains the constant value of $z=6:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}3+7t \\ -1-3t \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{z-6}{0}$ part and instead write $z=6$, as follows:

$$
\frac{x-3}{7}=\frac{y+1}{-3},\,z=6
$$

Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

r=[3−16]+t[7−30],t∈(−∞,∞)

a
x−37=y+1−3,z=6
b
x−73=y+3−1,z=0
c
x+37=y−1−3,z=−6
d
x+73=y−3−1,z=0
e
x−37=y+1−3=z−6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the usual formula, we get

x−37=y−(−1)−3=z−60=t,t∈(−∞,∞),

or equivalently

x−37=y+1−3=z−60,

which is problematic because z−60 involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the z component always maintains the constant value of z=6:

r=[3+7t−1−3t6],t∈(−∞,∞)

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the z−60 part and instead write z=6, as follows:

x−37=y+1−3,z=6

content.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
content.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-3}{7}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-3}=\frac{z-6}{0}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-3}{7}=\frac{y+1}{-3}=\frac{z-6}{0},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{z-6}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $z$ component always maintains the constant value of $z=6:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}3+7t \\ -1-3t \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{z-6}{0}$ part and instead write $z=6$, as follows:

$$
\frac{x-3}{7}=\frac{y+1}{-3},\,z=6
$$

r=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )

$$

after.html:
Question 15
?

Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

r=[−350]+t[702],t∈(−∞,∞)

a
x−37=z−22,y=5
b
x+37=z2,y=5
c
x−37=z2,y=5
d
x−37=z−21,y=5
e
x+32=z7,y=5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the usual formula, we get

x−(−3)7=y−50=z2=t,t∈(−∞,∞),

or equivalently

x+37=y−50=z2,

which is problematic because y−50 involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the y component always maintains the constant value of y=5:

r=[−3+7t52t],t∈(−∞,∞)

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the y−50 part and instead write y=5, as follows:

x+37=z2,y=5

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line When a Component of the Direction Vector is Zero
content.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation for the line with the following vector equation:

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$
content.worked_solution:
Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-(-3)}{7}=\frac{y-5}{0}=\frac{z}{2}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+3}{7}=\frac{y-5}{0}=\frac{z}{2},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{y-5}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $y$ component always maintains the constant value of $y=5:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-3+7t \\ 5 \\ 2t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{y-5}{0}$ part and instead write $y=5$, as follows:

$$
\frac{x+3}{7}=\frac{z}{2},\,y=5
$$

Question 16
?

Find a Cartesian equation of the straight line that passes through P(3,−5,7) and is parallel to v=⟨3,6,9⟩.

a
x+33=y+6−5=z+97
b
x+33=y−56=z+79
c
x−33=y−6−5=z−97
d
x−33=y+56=z−79
e
x3=y6=z9
Submit

decision.explanation: Using the point (3,-5,7) and direction (3,6,9), the canonical equation is (x-3)/3=(y+5)/6=(z-7)/9, matching option d.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Find a Cartesian equation of the straight line that passes through $P(3,-5,7)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨3,6,9⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

So, we have

$$
\frac{x-3}{3}=\frac{y-(-5)}{6}=\frac{z-7}{9}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\frac{x-3}{3}=\frac{y+5}{6}=\frac{z-7}{9}.
$$

Question 16

Find a Cartesian equation of the straight line that passes through P(3,−5,7) and is parallel to v=⟨3,6,9⟩.

a
x+33=y+6−5=z+97
b
x+33=y−56=z+79
c
x−33=y−6−5=z−97
d
x−33=y+56=z−79
e
x3=y6=z9
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point P(x0,y0,z0) and is parallel to the vector v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩, is given by x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vz=t,t∈(−∞,∞). So, we have x−33=y−(−5)6=z−79=t,t∈(−∞,∞) or, equivalently, x−33=y+56=z−79.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given Two Points on the Line
content.problem: Find a Cartesian equation of the straight line that passes through $P(3,-5,7)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨3,6,9⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

So, we have

$$
\frac{x-3}{3}=\frac{y-(-5)}{6}=\frac{z-7}{9}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\frac{x-3}{3}=\frac{y+5}{6}=\frac{z-7}{9}.
$$

Question 17
?

Find a Cartesian equation of the line shown in the figure above.

a
x+27=y−3−4=z−13
b
x+72=y+43,z=3
c
x+72=y+43=z−31
d
x+22=y−33=z−11
e
x7=y−4=z3
Submit

decision.explanation: The direction vector is Q-P=(5-(-2),-1-3,4-1)=(7,-4,3). Using P=(-2,3,1) gives (x+2)/7=(y-3)/(-4)=(z-1)/3, matching option a.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14042625/assets/1f9599192c1979f40fc519458019ed3296d9a5ef9048aaed41aab973c62e0be8.png)

Find a Cartesian equation of the line shown in the figure above.
after.worked_solution:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(-2,3,1)$ and $Q(5,-1,4).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. Let's consider the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ which is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨5,-1,4⟩-⟨-2,3,1⟩ \\  & =⟨7,-4,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point $P$ and the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$, we have that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the given line is given by

$$
\frac{x-(-2)}{7}=\frac{y-3}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{3}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+2}{7}=\frac{y-3}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{3}.
$$

Using the point P and the vector PQ→, we have that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the given line is given by x−(−2)7=y−3−4=z−13=t,t∈(−∞,∞), or equivalently x+27=y−3−4=z−13.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14042625/assets/1f9599192c1979f40fc519458019ed3296d9a5ef9048aaed41aab973c62e0be8.png)

Find a Cartesian equation of the line shown in the figure above.
content.worked_solution:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(-2,3,1)$ and $Q(5,-1,4).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. Let's consider the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ which is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨5,-1,4⟩-⟨-2,3,1⟩ \\  & =⟨7,-4,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point $P$ and the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$, we have that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the given line is given by

$$
\frac{x-(-2)}{7}=\frac{y-3}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{3}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+2}{7}=\frac{y-3}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{3}.
$$

\frac{x-7}{-6}=\frac{y+2}{3}=\frac{z-4}{0}.
$$

But the above equation is problematic because $\frac{z-4}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, in our line, the $z$ component always maintains the constant value of $z=4.$ For example, our two points $P(7,-2,4)$ and $Q(1,1,4)$ both have $z$-coordinates of $z=4.$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{z-4}{0}$ part and instead write $z=4,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x-7}{-6}=\frac{y+2}{3},\,z=4
$$

after.html:
Question 18
?

Find a Cartesian equation of the line shown in the figure above.

a
x−7−6=y+23,z=4
b
x−76=y−23,z=4
c
x−76=y−23,z=−4
d
x+7−6=y−2−3,z=−4
e
x+7−6=y+2−3,z=4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We know that the line passes through the points P(7,−2,4) and Q(1,1,4). Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. Let's consider the vector PQ→ which is given by PQ→=⟨1,1,4⟩−⟨7,−2,4⟩=⟨−6,3,0⟩.

Using the point P and the vector PQ→, we have that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the given line is given by x−7−6=y−(−2)3=z−40=t,t∈(−∞,∞), or equivalently x−7−6=y+23=z−40.

But the above equation is problematic because z−40 involves division by zero.

However, in our line, the z component always maintains the constant value of z=4. For example, our two points P(7,−2,4) and Q(1,1,4) both have z-coordinates of z=4.

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the z−40 part and instead write z=4, as follows:

x−7−6=y+23,z=4

content.worked_solution:
We know that the line passes through the points $P(7,-2,4)$ and $Q(1,1,4).$ Now, we need to find a vector parallel to the given line. Let's consider the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ which is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,1,4⟩-⟨7,-2,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-6,3,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point $P$ and the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$, we have that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the given line is given by

$$
\frac{x-7}{-6}=\frac{y-(-2)}{3}=\frac{z-4}{0}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-7}{-6}=\frac{y+2}{3}=\frac{z-4}{0}.
$$

But the above equation is problematic because $\frac{z-4}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, in our line, the $z$ component always maintains the constant value of $z=4.$ For example, our two points $P(7,-2,4)$ and $Q(1,1,4)$ both have $z$-coordinates of $z=4.$

So, in the Cartesian equation, we remove the $\frac{z-4}{0}$ part and instead write $z=4,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x-7}{-6}=\frac{y+2}{3},\,z=4
$$

None of the listed

decision.explanation: Using point (0,-1,3) and direction (2,3,-1), the Cartesian equation is x/2=(y+1)/3=(z-3)/(-1), matching option d.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem: Find a Cartesian equation of the straight line that passes through $P(0,-1,3)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,3,-1⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

So, we have

$$
\frac{x-0}{2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{3}=\frac{z-3}{-1}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x}{2}=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac{z-3}{-1}.
$$

Question 19
?

Find a Cartesian equation of the straight line that passes through P(0,−1,3) and is parallel to v=⟨2,3,−1⟩.

a
y−3−1=z+13,x=2
b
None of the listed
c
y−3−1=z+13,x=0
d
x2=y+13=z−3−1
e
x2=y3=z−1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point P(x0,y0,z0) and is parallel to the vector v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩, is given by x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vz=t,t∈(−∞,∞).

So, we have x−02=y−(−1)3=z−3−1=t,t∈(−∞,∞) or equivalently x2=y+13=z−3−1.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option d. Setting its ratios equal to t gives (x,y,z)=(2t,-1+3t,3-t), which passes through (0,-1,3) and has direction (2,3,-1). The observed incorrect submission selected e.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Line Given Two Points on the Line
content.problem: Find a Cartesian equation of the straight line that passes through $P(0,-1,3)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨2,3,-1⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

So, we have

$$
\frac{x-0}{2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{3}=\frac{z-3}{-1}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x}{2}=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac{z-3}{-1}.
$$

Question 20

Find a Cartesian equation of the straight line that passes through P(9,3,−7) and is parallel to v=⟨4,−5,3⟩.

a
x−94=y−3−5=z+73
b
x+94=y+3−5=z−73
c
x4=y−5=z3
d
x+49=y−53=z+3−7
e
x−49=y+53=z−3−7
Submit

decision.explanation: Using point (9,3,-7) and direction (4,-5,3), the Cartesian equation is (x-9)/4=(y-3)/(-5)=(z+7)/3, matching option a.

after.name: Question 20
after.problem: Find a Cartesian equation of the straight line that passes through $P(9,3,-7)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨4,-5,3⟩.$
after.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

So, we have

$$
\frac{x-9}{4}=\frac{y-3}{-5}=\frac{z-(-7)}{3}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-9}{4}=\frac{y-3}{-5}=\frac{z+7}{3}.
$$

content.problem: Find a Cartesian equation of the straight line that passes through $P(9,3,-7)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨4,-5,3⟩.$
content.worked_solution:
Remember that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the straight line that passes through the point $P({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ and is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$, is given by

$$
\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

So, we have

$$
\frac{x-9}{4}=\frac{y-3}{-5}=\frac{z-(-7)}{3}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x-9}{4}=\frac{y-3}{-5}=\frac{z+7}{3}.
$$
